subtype: Approach: follows friends into the same course without checking his own interest [Pitfall]
passage:
The counselling window closed at five, and it was already four. Arnab's finger hovered over the branch list on the college portal. Mechanical, electrical, civil: none had ever made his pulse jump. But Arohi and the whole group had ticked electronics, and choosing the same felt safe. He ticked electronics too and pressed submit with three minutes to spare.
Months into the second year, in a circuits class, he found himself watching the clock more than the board. The subjects were explained clearly, but he felt nothing for them. His friends were busy with problem sets they enjoyed, and he copied theirs just to keep up.

qa.q: When did the counselling window close?
qa.a: The counselling window closed at five.

qa.q: Why did Arnab tick electronics, and how did he feel about it later?
qa.a: Arnab ticked it because choosing what his friends chose felt safe, and later he felt nothing for the subjects.

qa.q: What could Arnab try now to find a better fit?
qa.a: Arnab could try a short project or talk to a senior in another branch, since checking his own interest is the step he skipped.

qa.q: How might Arohi and the group see Arnab's situation?
qa.a: Arohi and the friends enjoy their problem sets, so may not notice that Arnab is copying them and watching the clock.

grounding: A student picks the same engineering branch as his friends because it feels safe and later finds little interest.

subtype: Approach: tests borrowed methods on a small scale and keeps what fits [Revision]
passage:
Samir here. Last term Bidisha showed me her note-taking method, and my own notes were a mess, so I said I'd try it for one week. Only one.
The method has three parts: a summary box at the top of each page, colour codes for definitions, examples and doubts, and a margin for questions. On the first day the summary box made me stop and say the lecture in two lines, which showed me at once what I hadn't understood. The colour codes were another matter. Swapping pens took so long that I lost the lecturer's next sentence twice.
After a week I kept the box and the margin and dropped the colours. I told Bidisha the box was her best idea and the pens my worst habit.

qa.q: What three parts does the method have?
qa.a: The method has a summary box at the top of each page, colour codes for definitions, examples and doubts, and a margin for questions.

qa.q: What did Samir feel about the colour codes?
qa.a: Samir felt frustrated with them, since swapping pens took so long that the lecturer's next sentence was lost twice.

qa.q: What could Samir do to test another borrowed method?
qa.a: Samir could again try it for a short week and keep only the parts that help, since the summary box fit and the colour codes did not.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when hearing that only some of the method was kept?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel pleased that the summary box helped, and not offended, since Samir called it her best idea.

grounding: A student tries a friend's note-taking method for a week, keeps the summary box and drops the slowing colour codes.

subtype: Approach: copies a successful company's plan without its context [Pitfall]
passage:
Wasim: Three weeks, and we've hired nobody.
Yogesh: The process has four rounds. The big firm does it, so it must be right.
Wasim: The big firm has a hiring team of twenty. We are three people. Us, and Meena, who also does the invoices.
Yogesh: The aptitude test is ready, though. And the panel scoring sheet.
Wasim: Who is on the panel?
Yogesh: You and me.
Wasim: For a job we can barely pay for. Two candidates have already dropped out. One wrote that four rounds felt like an exam for a bigger company.
Yogesh: So what do you want, one chat?
Wasim: One conversation and one small task. We just need someone who can start on Monday.

qa.q: How many people work at the start-up?
qa.a: There are three people: Yogesh, Wasim and Meena.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh want to keep the four-round process?
qa.a: Yogesh believes that since the big firm does it, it must be right, and feels proud of the test and scoring sheet already prepared.

qa.q: What could the start-up do instead of copying the big firm?
qa.a: They could use one conversation and one small task, since a team of three needs someone who can start soon and cannot run a large process.

qa.q: How might a candidate see the four rounds?
qa.a: One candidate wrote that four rounds felt like an exam for a bigger company, so may find it discouraging for a small team.

grounding: A start-up copies a large firm's hiring process though it has three people and no budget, wasting weeks.

subtype: Approach: asks why something worked for them and what is different here [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday night. The rival's price for the cookie box is much lower than mine and their stall is always full. Before matching it, I made myself ask: why does that work for them?
Wrote it down. They sit on the station road with hundreds of office people passing, they buy flour by the sack, and they sell one thing. I'm in a residential lane. My customers are families who come twice a week, my butter costs more, and I bake six kinds.
So the same price would mean a much smaller gain for me. But their small, quick-to-grab box might suit parents on the weekend. Trying that first, at my own price.
Pavani

qa.q: Where is the rival's stall?
qa.a: The rival's stall is on the station road, with hundreds of office people passing.

qa.q: What did Pavani want to work out before copying the price?
qa.a: Pavani wanted to know why the price works for the rival, and felt careful and curious rather than hurried.

qa.q: What else could Pavani do if the weekend box does not sell?
qa.a: Pavani could ask regular families what they would buy, since their needs differ from the station crowd.

qa.q: How might families in the lane see the new small weekend box?
qa.a: Families who come twice a week might find a quick-to-grab box handy, though they may care more about the six kinds than the price.

grounding: Before copying a rival's pricing, Pavani asks what conditions made it work and adapts it to the local customers, costs and location.

subtype: Approach: thinks a task will take only a few minutes [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Yash. Before dinner I said, I'll finish this drawing in ten minutes. It was a big picture of a train station with lots of people. I did the platform first, then the train, then the little people, then the clouds. Then I looked at the clock and it had been one whole hour.
Mummy called, "Yash, dinner!" and I wasn't finished. I felt very upset and cross, and I said "Wait, wait!" too loudly. The drawing was still not done when I sat down, and my dinner was cold.
Next time I will not say ten minutes.

qa.q: How long did the drawing really take?
qa.a: The drawing took one whole hour.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Mummy called for dinner?
qa.a: Yash felt very upset and cross, because the drawing was not finished.

qa.q: What could Yash do next time before promising a time?
qa.a: Yash could guess a time for each part, such as the platform and the train, and add them up, since the whole picture had many parts.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the loud 'Wait, wait!'?
qa.a: Mummy had made dinner and called kindly, so may feel a bit hurt or tired when the answer comes back too loudly.

grounding: A child expects to finish a drawing in ten minutes, it takes an hour, and Yash is upset when called for dinner.

subtype: Approach: repeats the same underestimate again and again [Pitfall]
passage:
Bidisha: Vinita, what's the plan for this weekend?
Vinita: Revising all of chemistry. Saturday and Sunday. Done by Sunday night.
Bidisha: That's what you said about physics.
Vinita: This time it'll work. Physics had the visit to my aunt's.
Bidisha: How far did you get with physics?
Vinita: Half the chapters.
Bidisha: And biology before that?
Vinita: Also half. But chemistry is lighter.
Bidisha: Is it? There are fourteen chapters. The test is on Tuesday.
Vinita: I'll start at eight and go straight through. A weekend is enough.
Bidisha: You've said a weekend is enough three times now.
Vinita: It only failed because of things that happened.

qa.q: How many chapters does chemistry have?
qa.a: Chemistry has fourteen chapters.

qa.q: What does Vinita feel about the new weekend plan?
qa.a: Vinita feels confident it will work this time, and seems defensive about the earlier plans that stopped at half.

qa.q: What could Vinita try in place of one weekend for a whole subject?
qa.a: Vinita could look at how much was done last time and spread chemistry over several evenings, since half a subject is what a weekend has given before.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see the plan?
qa.a: Bidisha notices that physics and biology both stopped at half and that Vinita has said a weekend is enough three times, so worries the plan will fail again.

grounding: A teenager plans a whole subject's revision in one weekend, misses each time, and repeats the same plan for the next subject.

subtype: Approach: estimates from the best case and expects to finish early [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Parveen, and I sat next to Jasleen in the project lab for those two weeks. On the first Monday Jasleen said, "Three days, if nothing goes wrong," and started the report straight away.
By Wednesday the printer had jammed, the group chat was buzzing, and nobody could tell what the second step meant. On Friday the laptop would not turn on. Jasleen borrowed mine for a night. Then a teacher changed the format.
It ended up taking ten days. Jasleen looked tired and kept saying, "It should have been simple." I can't say what Jasleen was thinking, but the three-day number was never mentioned again.

qa.q: How many days did the report finally take?
qa.a: The report took ten days.

qa.q: What did Jasleen seem to feel at the end of the two weeks?
qa.a: Jasleen looked tired and kept saying it should have been simple, which suggests frustration, though Parveen cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do the next time a project needs an estimate?
qa.a: Jasleen could think of what usually goes wrong, such as breakdowns and unclear steps, and add time for it, since the best case rarely happens.

qa.q: How does Parveen see the ten days?
qa.a: Parveen watched from the next seat, lent a laptop, and cannot know Jasleen's thoughts, but saw that the three-day plan was never mentioned again.

grounding: A student estimates a project from the best case, and interruptions, a broken laptop and unclear steps stretch it to ten days.

subtype: Approach: uses past similar tasks to estimate time [Revision]
passage:
In Lagos, the sprint board showed a gap next to "export to PDF", and the product lead, Lindiwe, asked Emeka for an estimate. Emeka's first thought was three days.
Instead Emeka opened the tracker and found the last three features of the same size. They had taken five, eight and six days. The average was six. Emeka added two days for review and testing and typed, "Eight working days, likely."
Lindiwe raised her eyebrows. "That's longer than I hoped."
"It's what the last three actually took," said Emeka.
Lindiwe moved the release note by a week, and the feature shipped with a day to spare.

qa.q: How many days did the three earlier features take?
qa.a: They had taken five, eight and six days.

qa.q: What did Emeka think of the first idea of three days?
qa.a: Emeka treated it as a hopeful guess and did not trust it, preferring to check what had really happened.

qa.q: What else could Emeka do to make the estimate more reliable?
qa.a: Emeka could split the export feature into small parts and time each, since a breakdown shows extra steps a comparison can miss.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe react to the estimate?
qa.a: Lindiwe raised her eyebrows and said it is longer than hoped, but accepted it and moved the release note by a week.

grounding: A developer checks how long three similar features took, adds a margin and gives a realistic estimate.

subtype: Approach: splits a task into smaller parts and times each [Thinking]
passage:
Naledi had been asked to give a delivery date for the quarterly report. A week, she thought at first. That sounds right. But something nagged at her.
She took a sheet of paper and wrote the sections down: data cleaning, charts, analysis, summary, review. Then she guessed each one on its own. "Cleaning, two days. Charts, two. Analysis, three..." The numbers piled up, and the total came to nine working days.
"Nearly two weeks," she said aloud to the empty meeting room. She checked the sums twice, then walked to her manager's desk.
"Daniel, I gave you a week, but when I break it down it's closer to two. I wanted you to know now."
Daniel frowned, nodded, and moved the date on the plan.

qa.q: How many working days did the total come to?
qa.a: The total came to nine working days.

qa.q: What was Naledi feeling when she wrote the sections down?
qa.a: Naledi felt uneasy, since something nagged at her about the week she had first thought of.

qa.q: What could Naledi add to the plan after finding nine days?
qa.a: Naledi could add a few spare days for surprises, since even careful estimates can miss delays.

qa.q: How might Daniel see hearing this early?
qa.a: Daniel frowned at first but nodded and moved the date, so may be glad to know now instead of at the deadline.

grounding: Rather than guess a week for a report, she times each section separately, finds it takes nearly two, and tells her manager early.

subtype: Approach: friends make a plan and nobody questions the risks [Pitfall]
passage:
The plan came together in the canteen on Friday: five friends, a waterfall trail, Saturday afternoon, back by dark. Nobody mentioned that the bus left late or that the sky over the hills was already heavy.
Dhruv looked at the clouds and thought about wet rocks. Asif thought about the walk back in the dark. Each glanced round the table, everyone else was smiling, and each said nothing. "Great plan," someone said, and they clapped.
At the trailhead at four, thunder rolled in. The tea-stall owner shook his head. "The path shuts before dusk, and rain is coming."
They stood in silence until Asif said, "I was worried the whole way." "Me too," said Dhruv, and the others nodded. Dhruv called his father, and they waited under the stall's roof until he came. The fare was spent and nobody saw the waterfall.

qa.q: Where was the plan made?
qa.a: The plan came together in the canteen on Friday.

qa.q: What was Asif worried about while the group clapped?
qa.a: Asif was worried and uneasy about the walk back in the dark, and said nothing because everyone else was smiling.

qa.q: What could the friends have done at the canteen table?
qa.a: Any one of them could have said the worry aloud and suggested going earlier or another day, since several shared the same fear.

qa.q: How might the tea-stall owner see the group?
qa.a: The owner shook their head and warned about the path shutting before dusk, so probably sees a group who set out too late.

grounding: Friends plan a late waterfall trip and each privately worries about safety but assumes the rest are fine, so nobody questions the risks.
